stages.title: Advanced harmony
stages.hook: A progression leaves its key for four bars, then returns, and listeners feel the journey without knowing any theory. What tools make that possible?
explain: Functional harmony groups chords by role: tonic (I, vi) is stable, subdominant (IV, ii) moves away, and dominant (V, vii°) creates tension that resolves to the tonic. A secondary dominant is a dominant chord of a chord other than the tonic: in C major, D7 (D F♯ A C) is V7/V because it leads to G. Modal mixture borrows chords from the parallel minor, such as the A♭ major (♭VI) or F minor (iv) chord in C major.

Seventh and extended chords add colour. Built on C: Cmaj7 (C E G B), C7 (C E G B♭), Cm7 (C E♭ G B♭), Cø7 (C E♭ G♭ B♭) and the diminished seventh (C E♭ G♭ B♭♭). Adding the 9th, 11th or 13th (stacking more thirds) gives Cmaj9 and so on. The tritone substitution replaces V7 with the dominant seventh a tritone away: D♭7 for G7 in C, because both contain the same tritone (B/C♭ and F), resolving by half-step bass motion to C.

Modulation changes key. A pivot chord that belongs to both keys smooths it: A minor is vi in C and ii in G, so it can pivot from C to G. Chromatic chords such as the Neapolitan (♭II, first inversion, in C: D♭ F A♭ with F in the bass) and the augmented sixth (in C minor: A♭ C F♯ resolving outward to G) intensify cadences. These ideas come from European classical practice and are also used in jazz, pop and film music.

stages.title: Advanced composition
stages.hook: A 30-minute symphony can grow from four notes. How do composers turn tiny ideas into large structures?
explain: Large works depend on development: taking a motif and varying it by changing its rhythm, intervals, harmony, register, instrumentation or by fragmenting, inverting or lengthening it. Beethoven's Fifth Symphony (1808) builds a huge movement from a short four-note rhythmic motif.

Forms organise large-scale time. Sonata form has an exposition (themes in the tonic and a contrasting key, usually the dominant or relative major), a development (themes are transformed through many keys) and a recapitulation (themes return in the tonic). Rondo alternates a returning refrain with contrasting episodes (ABACA). Theme and variations changes one theme repeatedly. A fugue builds from imitation of a subject.

Twentieth-century composers extended these ideas. Arnold Schoenberg developed twelve-tone technique in the 1920s, using all twelve pitches in a row before any repeats. Minimalists such as Steve Reich and Philip Glass build music from small repeating patterns that change gradually. Composers in every tradition shape tension and release, plan climaxes and balance unity and variety.

stages.title: Orchestration
stages.hook: Ravel's Boléro repeats one melody and one rhythm for about fifteen minutes, yet it never gets dull. What changes?
explain: Orchestration is choosing instruments for musical ideas. Each instrument has a range, a timbre (tone colour) that changes with register, and dynamics that depend on pitch. Doubling a line with several instruments blends or brightens it; the same melody sounds different on flute, oboe or cello.

Know the transpositions. A B♭ clarinet or trumpet sounds a major second lower than written; an F horn sounds a perfect fifth lower; an E♭ alto saxophone sounds a major sixth lower; a piccolo sounds an octave higher and a double bass an octave lower than written. To get a concert pitch you must adjust each part.

Balance depends on register and numbers. Lower instruments need more weight to be heard; a solo flute can be covered by a tutti. Strings form the core of the orchestra, woodwinds colour, brass add power and percussion add rhythm and accent. Maurice Ravel's Boléro (1928) shows orchestration as the central interest: the same tune is passed among instruments and combinations while the volume grows. Orchestration is also essential in film scoring, brass band and big band writing.

stages.title: Music production and recording
stages.hook: A voice recorded in a cupboard can sound better than one in a big room. What does a producer actually control?
explain: Recording turns sound into signal. A microphone converts air pressure into an electrical signal; a preamp raises it; an audio interface converts it to digital by sampling. The sample rate is how many measurements per second (44.1 kHz for CDs, 48 kHz in video), and the bit depth is how finely each is measured (16-bit gives 65,536 levels, about 96 dB of dynamic range; 24-bit gives about 144 dB).

The Nyquist theorem says that a sample rate can capture frequencies up to half its value. So 44.1 kHz can capture up to 22.05 kHz, above the range of human hearing (about 20 Hz to 20 kHz). Gain staging means setting levels so the signal is strong but never clips (distorts at the maximum level).

In a digital audio workstation (DAW), tracks are edited and mixed. Mixing tools: EQ shapes frequency balance, compression reduces dynamic range, reverb adds space, panning places sounds left to right, and automation changes settings over time. Mastering is the final polish for consistent level and sound across platforms. MIDI is not audio but data about notes, so a sound can be changed afterwards. Producers work in all genres, from hip hop beat-making to orchestral film scoring.

example.q: What is the highest frequency a 48 kHz recording can represent?

stages.title: Jazz improvisation
stages.hook: A jazz soloist improvises over chord changes at high speed. What is going through their mind?
explain: The most common jazz building block is the ii–V–I progression. In C major it is Dm7 – G7 – Cmaj7. Players imagine a scale or mode for each chord: D Dorian over Dm7, G Mixolydian over G7 and C Ionian (major) over Cmaj7. Often they just use the same C major notes, but they target the chord tones.

Guide tones, the thirds and sevenths of each chord, show the harmony most clearly. In ii–V–I, the 7th of Dm7 (C) falls by half step to the 3rd of G7 (B), and the 7th of G7 (F) falls by half step to the 3rd of Cmaj7 (E). Bebop players added chromatic passing notes and arpeggios outlining chords, as heard in Charlie Parker's playing. Other tools: altered scales over dominant chords, tritone substitution, motivic development, rhythmic displacement and quoting.

Comping (accompanying) means chords and rhythms that support the soloist; rhythm sections respond to the soloist in real time. The swing feel treats paired eighth notes unequally. Great improvisers combine technical vocabulary, ear training and a sense of narrative. The same skills of listening and responding occur in other improvisational traditions.

stages.title: Classical composition and interpretation
stages.hook: Ten pianists can play the same notes by Chopin and sound entirely different. What decisions create the difference?
explain: Interpretation is how a performer realises a score. The notation tells pitches and approximate durations, but not everything: how much rubato (flexible tempo), how to shape a phrase, which voice to bring out, how to articulate and pedal. Interpretation begins with understanding structure, harmony, style and the composer's era.

Style matters. Baroque performance often uses ornaments (trills, mordents), dance rhythms and lighter articulation; historically informed performance uses period instruments and sources. In the Classical period balance and clarity matter. Romantic music asks for expressive tempo flexibility, large dynamic contrasts and rich tone. Editions differ, and an urtext edition aims to present the composer's own text with minimal editing.

Composition and interpretation work together. Beethoven's symphonies use motivic development; Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique (1830) is programme music, telling a story; Florence Price's Symphony in E minor was performed by the Chicago Symphony Orchestra in 1933. Performers study scores, listen to recordings critically, decide on a plan, and then respond to the room and audience. Interpretation can differ without being wrong when it is grounded in the score and style.

stages.title: Opera and vocal performance
stages.hook: Why does a Wagner soprano sound different from a Mozart soprano, even singing the same note?
explain: Opera singing demands a voice that carries over an orchestra without amplification. This depends on breath support, a relaxed larynx, vowel shaping and resonance, including the "singer's formant", a cluster of strong overtones around 3 kHz that helps the voice cut through. Vibrato is a regular small variation in pitch and loudness that gives richness.

Voices are classified by range, weight and colour (Fach). Sopranos can be coloratura (agile, high), lyric or dramatic (heavier). Male voices include tenor, baritone and bass; mezzo-soprano and contralto are lower female voices. Singers move between registers at passages called the passaggio, which needs technique to smooth.

Opera styles vary. Italian bel canto emphasises beautiful, agile line. Mozart's The Marriage of Figaro (1786) blends comedy and ensemble writing. Richard Wagner's works use leitmotifs, recurring musical themes tied to characters or ideas, and aim at a Gesamtkunstwerk, a total work of art. Bizet's Carmen (1875) is French. Beijing opera classifies roles as sheng (male), dan (female), jing (painted face) and chou (clown). Singers must also act, learn languages and work with directors and conductors; surtitles help audiences follow the text.

stages.title: Global musical traditions
stages.hook: Music in Lagos, Rio, Chennai, Cairo and Beijing can all be called "popular" or "classical". What do these traditions share, and what is unique?
explain: Africa: highlife grew in Ghana and Nigeria from local rhythms, brass bands and guitar; Nigerian bandleader Fela Kuti created Afrobeat in the late 1960s and 1970s by combining highlife, jazz, funk and Yoruba traditions, with long grooves and political lyrics. Afrobeats (with an s) is a newer pop sound from Nigeria and Ghana in the 2000s and 2010s. West African drumming often uses interlocking rhythms (polyrhythm) and call and response, which also shaped gospel, blues and hip hop in the Americas.

Americas: hip hop began in the Bronx, New York, in the 1970s with DJs such as DJ Kool Herc, MCs, breaking and graffiti. Salsa was shaped in New York by Cuban and Puerto Rican musicians from Afro-Cuban styles. Samba is central to Brazilian carnival; bossa nova arose in Rio in the late 1950s with João Gilberto and Antônio Carlos Jobim. Flamenco comes from Andalusia in southern Spain, with song (cante), guitar (toque), dance (baile) and handclaps (palmas). Indigenous North American music includes powwow drumming and song; Aboriginal Australian music includes songlines and the didgeridoo (yidaki).

Asia and the Middle East: Indian classical music has Hindustani and Carnatic traditions, built on raga (melodic framework) and tala (rhythmic cycle). Arabic maqam and Turkish makam use modes with intervals smaller than a semitone. Chinese music has traditional instruments such as the erhu and guzheng; Japanese traditional music includes gagaku (court music), koto and shakuhachi. Polynesia has chants, dance and log drums. Electronic dance music spans the world and its history includes Detroit techno and Chicago house in the 1980s.

stages.title: Advanced instrumental or vocal performance
stages.hook: Why do elite performers practise one bar for twenty minutes instead of playing the whole piece again and again?
explain: Effective practice is deliberate: set a specific goal, work on the hardest passages slowly, correct errors immediately, and test the result. Short, focused sessions with breaks beat long, unfocused ones. Slow practice builds accurate motor patterns; gradual speed-up uses a metronome. Record yourself and listen back critically.

Intonation and tone are core skills. In equal temperament the octave is divided into 12 equal semitones, each with frequency ratio 2^(1/12) ≈ 1.0595. If A4 = 440 Hz, E5 (seven semitones higher) is 440 × 2^(7/12) ≈ 659.3 Hz. A pure fifth (3:2) would be 660 Hz, close but slightly different. Singers and string and wind players adjust pitch by ear to blend. A cent is 1/100 of a semitone.

Performing also involves managing nerves, memory and stagecraft. Techniques include rehearsing in performance conditions, visualising, controlled breathing, reframing nerves as energy, and having a memory plan (harmonic, visual, and muscle memory). Ergonomics and warm-ups prevent injury; stop if you feel pain. Great performance combines technique, musical understanding and communication with the audience, whether in a concert hall, a village festival or a studio.
